title: A landscape of errors
text: A machine learning model makes predictions using adjustable numbers called parameters. Training means finding parameter values that reduce prediction error. To see how this works, imagine a model with just one parameter, called w. Each possible value has a corresponding loss. Plot those losses, and we get a landscape.

title: Find a local rule
text: In this simplified example, the loss is w minus three, squared. The lowest point occurs at three. We can see that because the whole curve is visible. But a training algorithm needs a rule it can apply from its current position. What information tells it which way to move?

title: The slope tells us the direction
text: The slope gives us that information. Here, the curve slopes downward as w increases, so moving right reduces the loss. On the other side, the slope is positive, so moving left helps. At the bottom, the slope is zero. The derivative measures this slope. With many parameters, the corresponding collection of derivatives is called the gradient.

title: Take one calculated step
text: Gradient descent moves opposite the gradient. Take the current parameter, subtract the gradient multiplied by a learning rate, and repeat. Starting at minus one, our slope is minus eight. With a learning rate of zero point two, the next parameter is zero point six. Subtracting a negative slope moves us right, toward lower loss.

title: Choose a controlled step
text: Repeat the same calculation, and the point approaches the bottom. The learning rate controls the size of each step. A small rate makes steady but slow progress. A suitable rate gets there faster. A rate that is too large can jump across the valley and move farther away. For this curve, positive rates below one converge. At one, the point oscillates. Above one, it moves farther away. A downhill direction does not guarantee a good step.

title: The same idea in more dimensions
text: Real models usually have many parameters. We can picture two of them as positions on a contour map. The gradient points toward the steepest local increase; its negative points toward the steepest local decrease. Complex landscapes may contain several valleys, so gradient descent does not guarantee the best possible solution. But the working rule stays the same: measure the slope, take a controlled step, and repeat.
